801.quote_or_event: “If after contracting a firm friendship with any one, I set myself to note his good and bad qualities, may I be cast into the hell where the traitor who discovers the secrets of his friend is punished, and may I be scoffed at by the whole world!”
801.explanation: The Jain didactic poet binds himself by an oath never to sit in judgement on a friend once the friendship is firmly made.
801.tie_back: The Kural defines old friendship as the bond that never belittles the freedoms an intimate friend takes, and the Naladiyar treats auditing a settled friend's conduct as a kind of treachery.
801.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
801._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. This is from a Tamil Jain didactic work, not canonical scripture, and it is about not scrutinising a friend's faults in general rather than about tolerating a friend's liberties in particular.

802.quote_or_event: “Though they do evil exceedingly, is it not fitting to be patient with one's friend? … the forbearance of one is the friendship of both.”
802.explanation: The poet makes forbearance the thing that holds a friendship together: when one friend bears with the other, both keep the bond.
802.tie_back: The Kural calls the freedoms of intimacy a structural part of friendship that the wise should welcome, and the Naladiyar likewise treats bearing with a friend as what friendship is made of.
802.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
802._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text, with a vocative address to a hill-chief left out at the ellipsis. Tamil Jain didactic verse; it speaks of forbearing a friend's wrongs, which is stronger than the Kural's welcoming of a friend's familiar freedoms.

803.quote_or_event: “Is it right utterly to abandon friends, who ought not to be forsaken though guilty of evil deeds? … will men cut off their hand because it has struck the eye?”
803.explanation: The poet compares a friend's offence to one's own hand striking one's own eye: nobody cuts off the hand, because it is part of oneself.
803.tie_back: The Kural asks what use an old friendship is if one will not accept a friend's act as though one had done it oneself, and the Naladiyar's image of the hand and the eye makes the friend's act literally one's own.
803.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
803._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text, with a descriptive address to a mountain-chief left out at the ellipsis. Tamil Jain didactic verse; the hand-and-eye image closely matches the Kural's 'as though one had done it oneself'.

804.quote_or_event: “In a thing done by strangers, though in itself exceeding bad, what is there fitted to give pain? Considered rightly, it is the acts of those who are affectionately attached; which, O lord of the land where the waterfalls murmur! will be esteemed excellent, abiding in the mind.”
804.explanation: The poet holds that the acts of those bound to us by affection are, rightly considered, treasured in the mind as excellent, unlike the acts of strangers.
804.tie_back: The Kural says the wise welcome what a close friend does unasked as something they wanted, and the Naladiyar similarly says a loving friend's acts are prized for the love behind them.
804.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
804._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. Tamil Jain didactic verse; the old translation's syntax is awkward, but its point that a friend's acts are valued because of the affection behind them closely fits the Kural.

805.quote_or_event: “But for the following fifteen good qualities he is called well-behaved: if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody; … if he listens to friendly advice; … if he is not angry with friends; if he speaks well even of a bad friend behind his back …”
805.explanation: Among the marks of a well-disciplined monk, the Uttaradhyayana lists not being angry with friends, not holding on to wrath, and speaking well even of a bad friend.
805.tie_back: The Kural asks us to put a friend's hurtful act down to ignorance or intimacy, not malice, and the Jain canon likewise asks the disciplined person not to be angry with friends and to speak kindly even of a friend who errs.
805.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.10–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
805._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, with some items left out at the ellipses. It is canonical and on the same theme of not resenting friends, but it gives no account of the two charitable explanations (ignorance or intimacy) that are the Kural's specific point.

806.quote_or_event: “Even though they do what is disagreeable, one should preserve as gold those who ought not to be forsaken. Daily do men seek for fire and keep it in their house, though it has consnmed both their good house and gold.”
806.explanation: The poet says that a true friend should be kept like gold even when he causes harm, just as people keep fire in the house though fire has burned houses and gold.
806.tie_back: The Kural says those who keep within friendship's bounds will not give up old friends even when the bond brings them loss, and the Naladiyar's fire that has cost house and gold yet is still kept is the same teaching.
806.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
806._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text; 'consnmed' is the source's own typo and is kept as printed. Tamil Jain didactic verse; very close to the Kural's idea of keeping a friend despite loss.

807.quote_or_event: “Men will not be angry, but be patient concerning the friendship of those whom they themselves have courted, though these persons act towards them with constant hate.”
807.explanation: The poet compares friends to good water that keeps bursting the bank yet is still drawn up: those who have chosen a friend stay patient even when the friend treats them harshly.
807.tie_back: The Kural says those whose friendship has come a long way through love do not stop loving even when friends bring them ruin, and the Naladiyar likewise asks patience toward chosen friends who repeatedly do harm.
807.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
807._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text (the stanza's second sentence, without the opening water simile). Tamil Jain didactic verse; it speaks of friends one has courted rather than specifically of long-standing ones.

808.quote_or_event: “Lord of the cool land where the waters brightly shine! the good will not look upon the faults of others after mixing with them (in friendship), though they act disagreeably. Persons destitute of strength of mind who take up evil things and speak of them after mixing (in friendship), are themselves inferior to those of whom they speak.”
808.explanation: The poet says that good people will not dwell on a friend's faults, and that those who gossip about a friend's failings are lower than the friend they talk about.
808.tie_back: The Kural praises the friend so secure in intimacy that he will not even listen to talk of his friend's faults, and the Naladiyar similarly puts the one who talks of a friend's faults below the friend himself.
808.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 7 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
808._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. Tamil Jain didactic verse; it is about not looking at or spreading a friend's faults, not about refusing to hear them from others or about the 'day of gain' when the trust is proved.

809.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
809.explanation: The poet contrasts quick attachments with the deep friendship that holds on to the memory of a friend even through long absence.
809.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves those who never let go of friends whose bond has come down unbroken through the years, and the Naladiyar likewise praises a friendship that is not abandoned over long years apart.
809.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
809._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. Tamil Jain didactic verse; it matches the unbroken old friendship but says nothing about the world's love for such people, which is half of the Kural.

810.quote_or_event: “As the virtuous Kitra, for old friendship's sake, loved the king who was attached to sensual pleasures, and as he had at heart his welfare, he spoke to him the following words”
810.explanation: The monk Citta, meeting King Brahmadatta, his brother and companion through several past births, keeps his old affection for him and seeks his good even though the king has given himself to sensual pleasures.
810.tie_back: The Kural praises those who never part from their goodwill toward old friends even when the friends go wrong, and Citta's continued love for a straying old companion is a canonical Jain example of that loyalty.
810.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.15, 'Citta and Sambhūta' (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
810._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, where the name is printed 'Kitra' and the verse number is mis-OCRed as '(is)', between verses 14 and 16. A strong fit for loyalty to an erring old friend, but the Kural's point that even enemies come to love such people has no parallel here.
